1.title: Performance
1.description: Jet performance, takeoff speeds, climb, cruise, descent, and landing

sections.title: Basic Parameters - Temperature
sections.content: Understanding temperature measurements is crucial for jet operations.
key_points: Total Air Temperature (TAT): Outside air temperature plus 100% Ram Rise
Ram Air Temperature (RAT): Outside air temperature plus a certain percentage of the ram rise
Static Air Temperature (SAT) or OAT: Free air temperature from ground sources or corrected TAT
Ram Rise: Increase in air temperature due to compressibility, negligible below 0.3 Mach

sections.title: Basic Parameters - Speeds
sections.content: Different airspeed measurements serve different purposes in flight operations.
key_points: Indicated Airspeed (IAS): Speed shown by aircraft instruments
Calibrated Airspeed (CAS): IAS corrected for position error
Equivalent Airspeed (EAS): CAS corrected for compressibility error
True Airspeed (TAS): EAS corrected for air density variation
Ground Speed (GS): TAS corrected for wind

sections.title: Basic Parameters - Altitudes
sections.content: Altitude measurements are fundamental to flight operations and separation.
key_points: Indicated Altitude: Altimeter reading with sub-scale set to QNH
Pressure Altitude: Height above Standard Datum Plane (29.92 inHg/1013.25 hPa)
Density Altitude: Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature
Absolute Altitude: Height above surface measured by radio altimeter
True Altitude: Actual height above sea level

sections.title: Takeoff Speeds
sections.content: Takeoff speeds are critical for safe aircraft departure.
key_points: VS (Stall Speed): Speed where airflow separates completely and wing fully stalls
VS1G: Speed at which airflow separation starts but not full wing stall
VMCA: Minimum inflight speed for control using aerodynamic controls only
VMCG: Minimum speed on ground for control using aerodynamic controls only
VMU: Lowest calibrated airspeed for safe liftoff without tail strike
VLOF: Speed at which airplane lifts off, depends on AoA, flaps, and weight
VMBE: Maximum speed for full braking to complete stop

sections.title: V1 - Decision Speed
sections.content: V1 is the critical decision speed for takeoff.
key_points: V1 is the speed used as reference whether to reject or continue takeoff
V1 is NOT a decision speed - it's the speed where first braking action must be applied
Decision to reject must be taken BEFORE V1
VMCG ≤ V1 ≤ VR and VMBE

sections.title: Rotation and Takeoff Climb Speeds
sections.content: VR and V2 are essential for safe takeoff execution.
key_points: VR: Speed at which airplane is rotated for liftoff, minimum 1.05 VMCA
V2: Takeoff climb speed at screen height, must be maintained with engine failure
V2 minimums: 1.2 VS or 1.13 VS1G, and VMCA
Screen height: 35ft for dry runway, 15ft for wet/contaminated

sections.title: Takeoff Performance
sections.content: Understanding takeoff performance calculations is essential for safe operations.
key_points: Critical Engine: Engine whose failure causes most adverse effects
Clearway: Area beyond runway with upward slope not exceeding 1.25%
Stopway: Area beyond runway able to support aircraft weight during aborted takeoff
TODR: Takeoff Distance Required - longest of engine failure or 115% all engines
ASDR: Accelerate-Stop Distance Required - accelerate to V1 then stop
TORR: Takeoff Run Required

sections.title: Field Lengths
sections.content: Field length calculations determine maximum takeoff weights.
key_points: Balanced Field Length: TODA equals ASDA (no clearway/stopway used)
Unbalanced Field Length: TODA not equal to ASDA (clearway/stopway used)
Balanced V1: Selected when TODR equals ASDR
RTOW: Regulated Takeoff Weight limited by structure, runway, tires, brakes, climb, obstacles

sections.title: Takeoff Path Segments
sections.content: The takeoff path consists of four distinct segments.
key_points: First Segment: From 35ft to gear retracted, using TO thrust and flaps at V2
Second Segment: From gear up to 400ft minimum, using TO thrust and flaps at V2
Third Segment: Horizontal distance to accelerate to final climb speed, retracting flaps
Fourth Segment: From end of third segment to 1500ft with flaps up, MCT

sections.title: Climb Gradient
sections.content: Climb gradient affects maximum allowable takeoff weights.
key_points: Climb gradient: Height gained per unit of horizontal distance
Second segment gross gradient: 2.4% for 2-engine aircraft
Second segment net gradient: 1.6% (gross minus 0.8%)
Factors: Configuration, V1, V2, engine thrust, gross weight

sections.title: Engine Ratings
sections.content: Engine thrust ratings determine performance capabilities.
key_points: Flat Rated Power: Maximum thrust based on ambient temperatures
TMAX: Maximum temperature for full thrust
TREF: Temperature where flat rated power begins to decrease
Factors affecting thrust: Pressure, temperature, humidity, airspeed

sections.title: Thrust Management
sections.content: Thrust reduction methods protect engines and save fuel.
key_points: Assumed Temperature Method (ATM/FLEX): Dictated temperature limits thrust
De-rate: Replacing full rated engine with lower thrust engine
Thrust reduction shall not exceed 25%
Benefits: Reduces cost, easy to calculate, always conservative

sections.title: Thrust Ratings
sections.content: Different thrust settings for different flight phases.
key_points: Takeoff Thrust: 5-10 minutes maximum, 10 minutes with engine failure
Go-Around Thrust: Same as max TO thrust, higher speeds
Maximum Continuous Thrust (MCT): Highest continuous thrust for engine failure
Maximum Climb Thrust: For en-route climb and step climb
Maximum Cruise Thrust: Maximum during cruise

sections.title: Climb Performance
sections.content: Climb performance affects fuel efficiency and flight time.
key_points: Best Angle of Climb (VX): Shortest distance to specific altitude
Best Rate of Climb (VY): Least time to specific altitude
Speed constraints: 250 KIAS below 10,000ft, 300 KIAS/0.78 Mach above
Emergency descent: 250 KIAS below 10,000ft

sections.title: Cruise Performance
sections.content: Cruise phase represents about 90% of any flight.
key_points: Load Factor: Lift produced relative to gross weight
Maneuver Margin: Ability of air to support aircraft weight at high altitudes
Buffet Boundaries: Speeds for low and high speed buffet
Coffin Corner: Altitude with no buffet margin and 1.0g load factor

sections.title: Range and Endurance
sections.content: Fuel efficiency is critical for airline operations.
key_points: Specific Range: Distance traveled per unit of fuel (SR = TAS/Total Fuel Flow)
Maximum Range Cruise (MRC): Speed for maximum fuel mileage
Long Range Cruise (LRC): Speed with 1% loss in SR but significant speed increase
Optimum Altitude: Altitude for best fuel mileage
Step Climb: Series of altitude gains to improve fuel economy

sections.title: Descent Performance
sections.content: Efficient descent planning saves fuel and time.
key_points: Method 1: Distance = altitude × 3 + 10 (NM)
Method 2: Altitude = distance × 3 - 30 (feet)
Wind correction: Add 3NM per 10 knots tailwind, subtract for headwind
Weight effect: Higher rate of descent for light weights at constant speed

sections.title: Landing Performance
sections.content: Landing performance calculations ensure safe arrival.
key_points: VREF: Landing reference speed = 1.3 × VS
Dry runway: Landing distance may not exceed 60% of effective runway length
Wet runway: At least 115% of dry runway landing distance
Approach climb gradient: 2.1% for 2-engine, 2.4% for 3-engine, 2.7% for 4-engine

2.title: Meteorology
2.description: Weather phenomena, atmospheric science, and weather services

sections.title: Atmosphere
sections.content: Understanding the atmosphere is fundamental to meteorology.
key_points: Troposphere: Where weather occurs, temperature decreases with altitude
Stratosphere: Above troposphere, temperature increases with altitude
Standard atmosphere: 15°C at sea level, decreases 2°C per 1,000ft
Pressure decreases with altitude at different rates

sections.title: Temperature Effects
sections.content: Temperature affects aircraft performance and weather patterns.
key_points: Higher temperature reduces engine performance
Density altitude increases with temperature
Temperature inversions can trap pollutants and fog
Lapse rate: Rate of temperature change with altitude

sections.title: Pressure Systems
sections.content: Pressure systems determine weather patterns.
key_points: High pressure: Generally fair weather, sinking air
Low pressure: Generally cloudy, rising air, precipitation
Fronts: Boundaries between air masses
Jet streams: High-altitude wind patterns

sections.title: Wind
sections.content: Wind patterns affect flight planning and operations.
key_points: Wind shear: Sudden change in wind speed or direction
Clear air turbulence: Turbulence without visible clouds
Mountain waves: Oscillations downwind of mountains
Thermal winds: Caused by temperature differences

sections.title: Clouds and Precipitation
sections.content: Cloud types indicate weather conditions.
key_points: Cumulus: Fair weather clouds, can develop into thunderstorms
Stratus: Layer clouds, can indicate fog or low ceilings
Cumulonimbus: Thunderstorm clouds, avoid at all costs
Precipitation types: Rain, snow, sleet, hail

sections.title: Thunderstorms
sections.content: Thunderstorms pose significant hazards to aviation.
key_points: Three stages: Cumulus, mature, dissipating
Hazards: Turbulence, hail, lightning, wind shear, microbursts
Avoid by at least 20 NM from severe thunderstorms
Never fly through a thunderstorm

sections.title: Icing
sections.content: Icing conditions require careful planning and awareness.
key_points: Structural icing: Ice accumulation on aircraft surfaces
Carburetor icing: Can occur even in warm temperatures
Icing conditions: Temperature between -20°C and 0°C with visible moisture
Anti-ice and de-ice systems are critical for safety

sections.title: Visibility
sections.content: Visibility affects takeoff, landing, and navigation.
key_points: RVR: Runway Visual Range - measured visibility on runway
Ceiling: Height of lowest broken or overcast cloud layer
VMC: Visual Meteorological Conditions - sufficient visibility
IMC: Instrument Meteorological Conditions - insufficient visibility

sections.title: Weather Services
sections.content: Various weather services provide information for flight planning.
key_points: METAR: Aerodrome routine meteorological report
TAF: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast
SIGMET: Significant meteorological information
AIRMET: Airmen's meteorological information
PIREPS: Pilot weather reports

3.title: Aerodynamics
3.description: High-speed aerodynamics, flight principles, and aircraft performance

sections.title: Basic Aerodynamics
sections.content: Fundamental principles of flight.
key_points: Bernoulli's principle: Pressure decreases as airspeed increases
Newton's third law: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
Lift: Force perpendicular to relative wind
Drag: Force opposing aircraft motion

sections.title: High Speed Aerodynamics
sections.content: Jet aircraft operate in compressible flow regime.
key_points: Subsonic: Below Mach 0.8
Transonic: Mach 0.8 to 1.2
Supersonic: Above Mach 1.2
Shock waves form as aircraft approaches speed of sound

sections.title: Mach Number
sections.content: Mach number is critical for jet operations.
key_points: Mach = TAS / Speed of sound
Speed of sound varies with temperature
Critical Mach number: Where first supersonic flow appears
Mach buffet occurs above critical Mach number

sections.title: Swept Wings
sections.content: Wing sweep delays compressibility effects.
key_points: Effective airspeed reduced by cosine of sweep angle
Allows higher cruise Mach numbers
Can cause tip stall at high angles of attack
Variable sweep wings optimize for different flight phases

sections.title: Boundary Layer
sections.content: Boundary layer characteristics affect drag and performance.
key_points: Laminar flow: Smooth, low drag but unstable
Turbulent flow: Rough, higher drag but more stable
Flow separation causes stall
Boundary layer control can improve performance

4.title: Flight Controls
4.description: Primary and secondary flight controls, hydraulic and electronic systems

sections.title: Primary Flight Controls
sections.content: Primary controls maneuver the aircraft about its axes.
key_points: Ailerons: Control roll about longitudinal axis
Elevator: Control pitch about lateral axis
Rudder: Control yaw about vertical axis
Modern aircraft use fly-by-wire systems

sections.title: Secondary Flight Controls
sections.content: Secondary controls modify flight characteristics.
key_points: Flaps: Increase lift for takeoff and landing
Slats: Delay stall at high angles of attack
Spoilers: Reduce lift and increase drag
Trim systems: Relieve control forces

sections.title: Hydraulic Systems
sections.content: Hydraulic power operates most flight controls in large aircraft.
key_points: Multiple redundant hydraulic systems
Hydraulic fluid transmits power
Pumps, actuators, and valves control flow
Emergency systems available if hydraulics fail

sections.title: Fly-By-Wire Systems
sections.content: Electronic control systems replace mechanical linkages.
key_points: Electrical signals replace mechanical cables
Flight computers process pilot inputs
Protection systems prevent dangerous maneuvers
Reduced weight and improved performance

5.title: Instrument Navigation
5.description: Navigation systems, ILS, VOR, GPS, and inertial navigation

sections.title: VOR Navigation
sections.content: VHF Omnidirectional Range is a primary navigation aid.
key_points: Provides radial information from station
Can fly radials TO or FROM station
DME provides distance information
Used for en-route and approach navigation

sections.title: ILS System
sections.content: Instrument Landing System provides precision approach guidance.
key_points: Localizer: Horizontal guidance to runway centerline
Glideslope: Vertical guidance for descent path
Marker beacons: Distance information during approach
Can be used in low visibility conditions

sections.title: GPS Navigation
sections.content: Global Positioning System provides precise positioning.
key_points: Satellite-based navigation system
Provides position, velocity, and time
WAAS improves accuracy for approaches
Primary navigation for modern aircraft

sections.title: Inertial Navigation
sections.content: Inertial Reference Systems provide autonomous navigation.
key_points: Uses accelerometers and gyroscopes
No external references required
Accumulates error over time
Combined with GPS for accuracy

sections.title: Area Navigation (RNAV)
sections.content: RNAV allows direct routing between waypoints.
key_points: Does not require flying directly over navaids
Uses multiple navigation sources
Reduces flight distance and time
Foundation for modern air traffic management

6.title: Weight and Balance
6.description: Aircraft weight management, center of gravity, and loading

sections.title: Weight Concepts
sections.content: Understanding weight is fundamental to safe operations.
key_points: Empty Weight: Aircraft with all permanent equipment
Basic Empty Weight: Empty weight plus unusable fuel and fluids
Maximum Ramp Weight: Maximum weight for ground operations
Maximum Takeoff Weight: Maximum weight for takeoff
Maximum Landing Weight: Maximum weight for landing

sections.title: Center of Gravity
sections.content: CG position affects aircraft stability and control.
key_points: CG must remain within approved limits
Forward CG: More stable but less maneuverable
Aft CG: Less stable but more maneuverable
CG changes with fuel burn and payload

sections.title: Loading Calculations
sections.content: Proper loading ensures safe flight operations.
key_points: Moment = Weight × Arm
Total moment divided by total weight = CG position
Balance chart simplifies calculations
Weight and balance must be verified before each flight

7.title: Flight Planning
7.description: Route planning, fuel planning, and flight documentation

sections.title: Route Planning
sections.content: Efficient route planning saves time and fuel.
key_points: Direct routing when possible
Consider weather and winds
Avoid restricted airspace
Plan for contingencies

sections.title: Fuel Planning
sections.content: Fuel planning is critical for flight safety.
key_points: Trip fuel: Fuel for planned flight
Reserve fuel: Additional fuel for contingencies
Alternate fuel: Fuel to reach alternate airport
Final reserve: Fixed amount for emergency

sections.title: Performance Planning
sections.content: Performance calculations ensure safe operations.
key_points: Takeoff performance at departure airport
Landing performance at destination
Climb and descent planning
Altitude and speed selection

8.title: Jeppesen
8.description: Jeppesen charts, planning, and navigation materials

sections.title: Chart Types
sections.content: Jeppesen provides various chart types for flight operations.
key_points: Airport diagrams: Layout and taxiways
Approach plates: Instrument approach procedures
En-route charts: Low and high altitude airways
Star charts: Standard Terminal Arrival Routes

sections.title: Chart Interpretation
sections.content: Understanding chart symbols is essential.
key_points: Colors indicate different information types
Symbols represent navigation aids and obstacles
Contours show terrain elevation
Holdings patterns and restrictions

9.title: ATC
9.description: Air traffic control procedures, communications, and regulations

sections.title: ATC Communications
sections.content: Clear communication with ATC is essential.
key_points: Standard phraseology for clear communication
Readback of critical instructions
Use correct frequencies
Maintain situational awareness

sections.title: Clearances
sections.content: ATC clearances authorize specific actions.
key_points: Route clearance: Authorized route to fly
Approach clearance: Authorization for approach
Hold clearance: Instructions for holding
SID/STAR: Standard departures and arrivals

sections.title: Airspace Classes
sections.content: Different airspace classes have different requirements.
key_points: Class A: IFR only, FL180 and above
Class B: Busy airports, IFR and VFR with clearance
Class C: Towers with radar, IFR and VFR with radio contact
Class D: Towers without radar, VFR with radio contact
Class E: Controlled airspace, IFR and VFR
Class G: Uncontrolled airspace

10.title: Propulsion System
10.description: Gas turbine engines, fuel systems, and engine operations

sections.title: Gas Turbine Engine
sections.content: Jet engines operate on the Brayton cycle.
key_points: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow - intake, compression, combustion, exhaust
Turbojet: Basic jet engine
Turbofan: Bypass air for efficiency and noise reduction
Turboprop: Turbine drives propeller

sections.title: Engine Components
sections.content: Understanding engine components is essential for operations.
key_points: Compressor: Increases air pressure
Combustion chamber: Fuel burns with compressed air
Turbine: Extracts energy to drive compressor
Nozzle: Accelerates exhaust gases

sections.title: Engine Systems
sections.content: Various systems support engine operation.
key_points: Fuel system: Delivers fuel to engines
Ignition system: Starts combustion process
Oil system: Lubricates and cools engine
Bleed air: Compressed air for various uses

sections.title: Engine Monitoring
sections.content: Monitoring engine parameters ensures safe operation.
key_points: EGT: Exhaust Gas Temperature
N1: Low pressure compressor speed
N2: High pressure compressor speed
Fuel flow: Rate of fuel consumption
